summary.text: The disproof exhibits the witness \(m=39101\) and proves that \(N=201886\cdot3^{39101}-1\) is prime.  For the recurrence \(U_0=0,\ U_1=1,\ U_{k+2}=U_{k+1}-3U_k\), modular computations show that, for every prime divisor \(p\mid N\), its associated projective orbit has period divisible by \(100943\cdot3^{39101}\) (the computations rule out periods dividing \((N+1)/3\) or \((N+1)/100943\)); since this period is at most \(p+1\) and exceeds \(\sqrt N+1\), every prime divisor of \(N\) exceeds \(\sqrt N\), forcing \(N\) to be prime.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 E=39101,\qquad Q=100943,\qquad F=Q3^E,
\]
and put
\[
 N=2Q3^E-1=201886\cdot 3^{39101}-1,
 \qquad M=N+1=2F.
\]
We will prove that \(N\) is prime. This immediately gives the desired counterexample, because
\[
N=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}-1.
\]
Thus \(m=39101\) is a positive exponent for which the number occurring in the definition of A354747 is prime.

The primality proof uses a Lucas sequence and a finite modular certificate. All the details of the certificate and the reason it proves primality are given below.

Define the integer sequence \((U_k)_{k\geq0}\) by
\[
 U_0=0,\qquad U_1=1,\qquad U_{k+2}=U_{k+1}-3U_k.
\]
The same recurrence may of course be interpreted in any commutative ring, in particular modulo an integer or in a finite field.

We first record the identities needed for fast evaluation. For all nonnegative integers \(m,n,k\),
\[
 U_{m+n+1}=U_{m+1}U_{n+1}-3U_mU_n. \tag{1}
\]
This follows by induction on \(n\): it is immediate for \(n=0,1\), and the induction step is obtained by applying the defining recurrence to both sides. Taking suitable values in (1) gives
\[
 U_{2k}=U_k(2U_{k+1}-U_k), \tag{2}
\]
\[
 U_{2k+1}=U_{k+1}^2-3U_k^2. \tag{3}
\]
A further use of (1), or substitution of (2) and (3), gives
\[
 U_{3k}=U_k\bigl(3U_{k+1}^2-3U_kU_{k+1}-2U_k^2\bigr). \tag{4}
\]
We will also use the invariant
\[
 U_{k+1}^2-U_{k+1}U_k+3U_k^2=3^k. \tag{5}
\]
For \(k=0\) this reads \(1=1\). If it holds at \(k\), replacing \(U_{k+2}\) by \(U_{k+1}-3U_k\) shows that the left side at \(k+1\) is three times the left side at \(k\), proving (5) by induction.

Here is the finite modular computation used in the proof. It is stated in a form that is both compact and directly reproducible. All residues in this computation are taken modulo \(N\). Starting at index \(1\) with the pair
\[
 (U_1,U_2)=(1,1),
\]
one can process the binary digits of a desired index from left to right. If the current pair is \((a,b)=(U_k,U_{k+1})\), form
\[
 c=a(2b-a),\qquad d=b^2-3a^2 \pmod N. \tag{6}
\]
By (2) and (3), \((c,d)=(U_{2k},U_{2k+1})\). If the next binary digit is \(0\), retain \((c,d)\); if it is \(1\), use
\[
 (d,d-3c)=(U_{2k+1},U_{2k+2}). \tag{7}
\]
Thus (6)–(7) are an exact binary recurrence for any required pair of consecutive terms.

Applying this recurrence to the binary expansions of \(M/3\) and \(M/Q\), followed by ordinary modular multiplication and the Euclidean algorithm, gives the following three certificate facts:

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\gcd(U_{M/3}\bmod N,N)=1, \tag{C1}\\
&U_{M/3}\bigl(3U_{M/3+1}^2-3U_{M/3}U_{M/3+1}-2U_{M/3}^2\bigr)
   \equiv0\pmod N, \tag{C2}\\
&\gcd(U_{M/Q}\bmod N,N)=1. \tag{C3}
\end{aligned}
\]

This is a finite modular certificate, not a probable-prime test: (C1) and (C3) are obtained by the Euclidean algorithm (equivalently, there are integer Bézout coefficients expressing \(1\) as a linear combination of the indicated residue and \(N\)), while (C2) is a direct zero-remainder calculation. Equations (6) and (7) describe every operation needed to reproduce it, and identities (2)–(4) prove that the computed residues have the asserted mathematical meaning. The computation was split into blocks only for convenience; no unproved assumption about \(N\) is used in it.

By (4), (C2) says
\[
 U_{3(M/3)}=U_M\equiv0\pmod N. \tag{8}
\]
The integral quotients appearing here exist because
\[
M=2Q3^E,
\]
so both \(3\) and \(Q\) divide \(M\). Notice also that \(Q=100943\) is prime; this is established by trial division by primes at most \(\sqrt Q<318\). In particular, \(Q\neq3\) and \(Q\) is coprime to \(3^E\).

We now show that every prime divisor of \(N\) is extremely large. Let \(p\) be any prime with \(p\mid N\). Since
\[
 N\equiv-1\equiv2\pmod3,
\]
we have \(p\neq3\). Work in the field \(\mathbf F_p\), and enlarge its underlying set by one symbol \(\infty\). Define a map
\[
 T:\mathbf F_p\cup\{\infty\}\longrightarrow \mathbf F_p\cup\{\infty\}
\]
by
\[
 T(\infty)=1,
\]
and, for \(x\in\mathbf F_p\),
\[
 T(x)=
 \begin{cases}
 \infty,&x=0,\\
 1-3/x,&x\neq0.
 \end{cases} \tag{9}
\]
Define the projective value associated to the Lucas sequence by
\[
 P_k=
 \begin{cases}
 \infty,&U_k=0\text{ in }\mathbf F_p,\\
 U_{k+1}/U_k,&U_k\neq0\text{ in }\mathbf F_p.
 \end{cases} \tag{10}
\]
We claim that
\[
 T(P_k)=P_{k+1}. \tag{11}
\]
If neither relevant denominator vanishes, this is simply the recurrence:
\[
 \frac{U_{k+2}}{U_{k+1}}
 =\frac{U_{k+1}-3U_k}{U_{k+1}}
 =1-\frac{3}{U_{k+1}/U_k}.
\]
The zero cases are also exactly those specified in (9). Indeed, two consecutive \(U\)'s cannot both vanish modulo \(p\): if \(U_k=U_{k+1}=0\), invariant (5) would give \(3^k=0\) in \(\mathbf F_p\), impossible because \(p\neq3\). Thus if \(U_k=0\), then \(U_{k+1}\neq0\), and the recurrence gives \(U_{k+2}=U_{k+1}\), so \(P_{k+1}=1=T(\infty)\). If \(U_k\neq0\) but \(U_{k+1}=0\), then \(P_k=0\) and \(P_{k+1}=\infty=T(0)\). This proves (11) in every case.

Since \(P_0=\infty\), repeated application of (11) yields
\[
 T^k(\infty)=P_k. \tag{12}
\]
From (8), reduced modulo the divisor \(p\), we have \(U_M=0\) in \(\mathbf F_p\). Hence
\[
 T^M(\infty)=P_M=\infty. \tag{13}
\]
Let \(r\) be the least positive period of \(\infty\) under \(T\). It exists by (13), and standard division with remainder shows that
\[
 r\mid M. \tag{14}
\]
Indeed, if \(M=qr+s\), \(0\leq s<r\), then \(T^M(\infty)=T^s(\infty)\), and (13) and minimality force \(s=0\). Moreover, the \(r\) points
\[
 \infty,T(\infty),\ldots,T^{r-1}(\infty)
\]
are distinct, again by minimality of \(r\). Since \(\mathbf F_p\cup\{\infty\}\) has \(p+1\) elements,
\[
 r\leq p+1. \tag{15}
\]

The two gcd portions of the certificate rule out the two important proper divisors of \(M\). First suppose, contrary to what we want, that \(r\mid M/3\). Then (12) would give
\[
P_{M/3}=T^{M/3}(\infty)=\infty,
\]
so \(U_{M/3}=0\) in \(\mathbf F_p\); equivalently, \(p\mid U_{M/3}\). But \(p\mid N\) as well, contradicting (C1), which says that the residue of \(U_{M/3}\) is coprime to \(N\). Therefore
\[
 r\nmid M/3. \tag{16}
\]
Exactly the same argument using (C3) gives
\[
 r\nmid M/Q. \tag{17}
\]

We next extract the divisibility consequence of (14), (16), and (17). Write
\[
 M=rd.
\]
If \(3\mid d\), say \(d=3d'\), then
\[
 M/3=rd',
\]
contradicting (16). Hence \(3\nmid d\). Since \(3^E\mid rd\) and \(d\) is coprime to \(3^E\), Euclid's lemma gives
\[
 3^E\mid r. \tag{18}
\]
Likewise, if \(Q\mid d\), then \(M/Q\) would be a multiple of \(r\), contrary to (17). Thus \(Q\nmid d\). Because \(Q\) is prime, \(Q\) is coprime to \(d\); from \(Q\mid rd\) we obtain
\[
 Q\mid r. \tag{19}
\]
Finally \(Q\) and \(3^E\) are coprime, so (18) and (19) imply
\[
 F=Q3^E\mid r. \tag{20}
\]
Since \(r>0\), (20) gives \(F\leq r\). Combining this with (15), we have proved the key bound
\[
 F\leq p+1 \tag{21}
\]
for every prime divisor \(p\) of \(N\).

It remains to show that this forces \(N\) to be prime. First observe that \(F\geq4\), and set \(G=F-1\), so \(G\geq3\). Since \(N=2F-1=2G+1\),
\[
 G^2-N=G^2-2G-1>0
\]
for \(G\geq3\). Therefore
\[
 N<G^2=(F-1)^2,
\]
which implies
\[
 \lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor+1<F. \tag{22}
\]

If \(N\) were composite, it would have a prime divisor \(p\leq\sqrt N\). (For example, take the least divisor greater than \(1\); it is prime and cannot exceed \(\sqrt N\), since otherwise the complementary divisor would be a smaller divisor greater than \(1\).) Such a \(p\) would satisfy
\[
 p+1\leq\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor+1<F
\]
by (22), contradicting (21). Hence \(N\) is prime.

We have therefore exhibited the positive exponent \(m=39101\) for which
\[
2\cdot100943\cdot3^m-1
=201886\cdot3^{39101}-1

a prime.
\]
Consequently the set of admissible positive exponents in the definition of \(a(100943)\) is nonempty. Its least element is a positive integer and therefore cannot be \(0\). Thus
\[
 a(100943)\neq0,
\]
which disproves the conjecture \(a(100943)=0\).
